title: The iOS Crash We Could Not Reproduce
gist: A first-person postmortem of an intermittent SIGBUS crash in a large consumer iOS app, traced via ~10 experimental builds on one reproducing device to NSAttributedString HTML import running off the main thread; the fix was a shared @MainActor helper, and the key lesson is that a falling crash rate does not prove a concurrency bug is fixed.

insights.claim: The crash's root cause was converting HTML data to an NSAttributedString from an asynchronous screen-preparation path without guaranteed main-thread execution, even though Apple's HTML importer must not be called from a background thread.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Legacy framework constraints hidden behind modern Swift APIs remain a production reliability risk for large iOS apps.
insights.locator: The critical issue was that HTML-to-attributed-string conversion

insights.claim: Apple documents that HTML import via NSAttributedString may try to synchronize with the main thread, fail and time out, and WebKit handles the HTML conversion, so the call is not a pure data transformation.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: API surfaces that look pure but embed WebKit/main-thread dependencies are a recurring class of iOS defect.

insights.claim: The author argues a Swift initializer can look safe while hiding behaviour inherited from Objective-C, Foundation, UIKit, WebKit or run loops, and Swift concurrency does not automatically make underlying APIs safe for concurrent use.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Migration to Swift concurrency does not retire legacy-API risk; expect continued demand for concurrency-safety tooling.
insights.locator: The incident also changed how I evaluate framework abstractions

insights.claim: SIGBUS is a low-level invalid-memory-access signal that indicates a failure category, not a diagnosis, so it should not be read as proof of a specific memory-management cause.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Crash triage that over-interprets signals wastes engineering time on wrong hypotheses.
insights.locator: SIGBUS is a low-level invalid memory access signal

insights.claim: A defensive first hotfix noticeably reduced the app's overall crash rate while the target crash signature persisted, because lifecycle and synchronization changes altered timing without removing the unsupported execution context.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Aggregate stability metrics can mask unfixed defects; monitor specific crash signatures separately.
insights.quote: A lower overall crash rate does not prove that the root cause is fixed.
insights.locator: Why the First Hotfix Misled Us

insights.claim: Timing-dependent concurrency defects can survive many successful runs: two users with identical HTML calling the same function may hit the importer under different scheduling, making the crash appear random.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Intermittent production crashes may be scheduling-sensitive contract violations rather than data bugs.
insights.quote: changing the probability of a concurrency failure is not the same as removing its cause

insights.claim: Standard tools — Zombie Objects, exception and symbolic breakpoints, ownership review — failed to locate the crash, and neither developers nor QA could reproduce it consistently.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Conventional debugging has limits for intermittent concurrency faults; budget for experimentation.

insights.claim: The turning point was a QA engineer's device that reproduced the crash intermittently (every four or five attempts), turning production forensics into an experiment with a practical test oracle.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Preserving any reproducing environment is more valuable than adding speculative code changes.
insights.locator: A Reproducible Device Changed the Investigation

insights.claim: By asking which code had to remain for the crash to survive and removing one view or behaviour per build, the author narrowed the failure to one file after six or seven builds and then to one line, across roughly nine or ten experimental IPAs.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Systematic elimination builds are a reusable technique for unreproducible production incidents.

insights.claim: Confidentiality policies prevented sharing source or debugging artifacts with Stack Overflow, Apple Developer Forums or LinkedIn groups, so community help could not diagnose the issue.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Proprietary-code constraints limit outside help for enterprise incidents, raising the value of internal diagnostic capability.
insights.locator: I also explored potential solutions through developer communities

insights.claim: Rather than patching one call site, the author routed every HTML-to-attributed-string conversion through a shared @MainActor helper, turning a framework threading rule into a code-level boundary while leaving networking and decoding asynchronous.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Encoding platform contracts in shared abstractions prevents regression across large codebases.
insights.quote: A shared main-actor abstraction is a stronger safeguard than asking every call site to remember a framework threading rule.
insights.locator: Turning the Fix Into an Application Wide Guarantee

insights.claim: The fix was confirmed by three validations: the reproducing device stopped crashing, all related call sites used the helper, and post-release monitoring showed the targeted signature no longer appeared at a meaningful rate.
insights.speaker: Abhishek Gang Deb
insights.so_what: Multi-signal validation (repro, code audit, production telemetry) is the bar for declaring concurrency bugs fixed.
